EXT_G4_FP_2020_006.q: How many diameters of a circle can be drawn from one point on the circle?
hints: Think about what makes a line a diameter. It has to pass through one special point of the circle.
A diameter starts on the circle, passes through the centre, and ends on the circle. From your point, how many straight lines go through the centre?

Similar example: how many radii can be drawn from the centre of a circle? A radius joins the centre to a point on the circle. There are endless points on the circle, so endless radii can be drawn from the centre.
steps: A diameter is a straight line that joins two points on the circle and passes through the centre.
Start at the chosen point on the circle. To be a diameter, the line must go straight through the centre.
Only one straight line can pass through two fixed points, here the chosen point and the centre.
So only 1 diameter can be drawn from a point on the circle.

EXT_G4_FP_2021_024.q: The area of a circle is 3 times its circumference. What is the radius?
hints: This is a circle problem that uses two formulas: area equals pi times r times r and circumference equals 2 times pi times r. Compare the two.
Write 3 times the circumference: 3 times 2 times pi times r. Then set it beside the area, pi times r times r, and see what r must be.

Similar example: the area of a circle is 2 times its circumference. 2 times the circumference is 2 times 2 times pi times r, which is 4 times pi times r. The area is pi times r times r. Both have pi times r, so the other r must be 4. The radius is 4.
steps: The area of a circle is pi times r times r. The circumference is 2 times pi times r.
3 times the circumference is 3 times 2 times pi times r, which is 6 times pi times r.
So pi times r times r is the same as 6 times pi times r. Both sides have pi times r, so the r that is left must equal 6.
The radius is 6.

EXT_G4_FP_2022_020.q: The circumference and the area of a circle are numerically the same. What is the diameter?
hints: This is a circle problem with two formulas: circumference equals 2 times pi times r and area equals pi times r times r. Compare them, and read carefully whether the radius or the diameter is asked.
Set 2 times pi times r beside pi times r times r. Both have pi times r. See what the remaining r must be, and remember the question asks for the diameter.

Similar example: the area of a circle is 5 times its circumference. 5 times the circumference is 5 times 2 times pi times r, which is 10 times pi times r. The area is pi times r times r, so r must be 10. The diameter is 2 times 10, which is 20.
steps: The circumference is 2 times pi times r. The area is pi times r times r.
They are equal. Both have pi times r, so the r that is left must equal 2. The radius is 2 centimetres.
The diameter is twice the radius. 2 times 2 equals 4.
The diameter is 4 centimetres.

EXT_G4_FP_2022_033.q: Eight equal circles are drawn inside a rectangle in 2 rows of 4. Each circle touches the circles next to it and the nearest sides of the rectangle at one point only. The radius of each circle is 7 centimetres. What is the area of the rectangle?
hints: The circles fill the rectangle exactly, so its length and breadth can be counted in circle widths. The width of a circle is its diameter.
Find the diameter of one circle: it is twice the radius of 7 centimetres. The length of the rectangle is 4 diameters and the breadth is 2 diameters.

Similar example: 10 equal circles of radius 2 centimetres sit in a rectangle in 2 rows of 5. The diameter is 4 centimetres. The length is 5 times 4, which is 20 centimetres and the breadth is 2 times 4, which is 8 centimetres, so the area is 20 times 8, which is 160 square centimetres.
steps: The diameter of each circle is twice the radius. 2 times 7 equals 14.
The length holds 4 circles side by side. 4 times 14 equals 56.
The breadth holds 2 circles. 2 times 14 equals 28.
Area is length times breadth. The area of the rectangle is 1568 square centimetres. 56 times 28 equals 1568.

EXT_G4_FP_2023_033.q: The circumference of a circle is 132 centimetres. Find its area.
hints: This is a circle problem in two parts. Use the circumference to find the radius, then use the radius to find the area. Take pi as 22 over 7.
Circumference equals 2 times pi times r. Put 132 for the circumference and 22 over 7 for pi, and find r.

Similar example: a circle has circumference 44 centimetres. With pi as 22 over 7, the circumference is 44 over 7 times r, so r is 44 times 7 divided by 44, which is 7 centimetres. The area is 22 over 7 times 7 times 7, which is 154 square centimetres.
steps: Circumference equals 2 times pi times r. With pi as 22 over 7, this is 44 over 7 times r.
So r is 132 times 7 divided by 44. The radius is 21 centimetres.
Area equals pi times r times r. 22 over 7 times 21 times 21 equals 1386.
The area is 1386 square centimetres.

EXT_G4_FP_2025_015.q: The circumference of a circle equals the perimeter of a rectangle, 14 centimetres by 8 centimetres. What is the radius?
hints: This problem joins two shapes. Find the perimeter of the rectangle first, then use the circumference formula, 2 times pi times r, with pi as 22 over 7.
Work out the perimeter of the rectangle: 2 times, length plus breadth. That number is also the circumference of the circle.

Similar example: a circle's circumference equals the perimeter of a rectangle 50 centimetres by 38 centimetres. The perimeter is 2 times, 50 plus 38, which is 176 centimetres. With pi as 22 over 7, the circumference is 44 over 7 times r, so r is 176 times 7 divided by 44, which is 28 centimetres.
steps: Find the perimeter of the rectangle. 2 times, 14 plus 8, equals 44.
The circumference is also 44 centimetres. Circumference equals 2 times pi times r, which is 44 over 7 times r when pi is 22 over 7.
So r is 44 times 7 divided by 44. 44 times 7 divided by 44 equals 7.
The radius is 7 centimetres.

EXT_G4_WS2_CH21_001.q: The distance from the centre of a circle to any point on the circle is called the:
hints: This is about the parts of a circle. Each part has its own name. Think about which one starts at the centre.
Picture a line drawn from the centre straight out to the edge of the circle. It goes only halfway across.
Similar example: a line that joins two points on a circle and passes through the centre goes all the way across. It is called the diameter.
steps: Mark the centre of a circle and any point on the circle.
The line joining them goes from the centre to the edge. Every such line has the same length.
This distance is called the Radius.

EXT_G4_WS2_CH21_002.q: The diameter of a circle is:
hints: This is about the parts of a circle. Think about how the radius and the diameter are drawn.
Draw a diameter and mark the centre on it. Count how many radii lie along that diameter.
Similar example: a circle has diameter 12 centimetres. The centre cuts the diameter into two equal pieces, and each piece is a radius. So the radius is 12 divided by 2, which is 6 centimetres.
steps: A diameter goes across the circle through the centre.
The centre cuts it into two pieces, and each piece is a radius.
So the diameter is Twice the radius.

EXT_G4_WS2_CH21_003.q: The longest chord of a circle is the:
hints: This is about the parts of a circle. A chord is a straight line joining two points on the circle.
Picture chords drawn across a circle. They get longer as they move closer to the centre. Where is the longest one?
Similar example: in a circle with centre O, chord P Q passes through O and chord R S does not. P Q is made of two radii end to end, so it is as long as a chord can be. R S is shorter.
steps: A chord joins two points on the circle.
Chords get longer as they get closer to the centre. The longest one passes through the centre.
A chord through the centre is called a diameter. So the longest chord is the Diameter.

EXT_G4_WS2_CH21_004.q: If the radius of a circle is 7 centimetres, what is its diameter?
hints: This is about the radius and the diameter of a circle. Think about how the two are related.
The diameter goes right across the circle through the centre, so it is made of two radii. Use the radius of 7 centimetres.
Similar example: a circle has radius 9 centimetres. The diameter is twice the radius, so it is 2 times 9, which is 18 centimetres.
steps: The diameter is twice the radius.
Multiply the radius by 2. 2 times 7 equals 14.
The diameter is 14 centimetres.

EXT_G4_WS2_CH21_005.q: The boundary of a circle is called the:
hints: This question is about the names of the parts of a circle. Think about which word means the line that goes all the way around.
Picture walking along the edge of a round park until you are back where you started. Which word names that whole path around?
A similar example: the line going all the way around a square is called its perimeter. A circle has its own special word for the distance all the way around.
steps: The boundary of a circle is the curved line that goes all the way around it.
The length of that line has a special name. It is like a perimeter, but for a circle.
The boundary of a circle is called the circumference.

G4A_CIRCLE_001.q: The diameter of a circular plate is 18 centimetres. What is its radius?
hints: Think about how the radius and the diameter of a circle are related.
The radius is half of the diameter. Find half of 18.
Example: A circle has diameter 10 centimetres. Its radius is 10 divided by 2, which is 5 centimetres.
steps: The radius goes from the centre to the circle. The diameter goes right across through the centre, so it is two radii.
Halve the diameter. 18 divided by 2 equals 9.
The radius is 9 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_002.q: Kiran wants to draw a circle of diameter 12 centimetres with a compass. How far apart should the needle point and the pencil tip be?
hints: The needle of a compass sits at the centre and the pencil draws the circle. Think about which length that is.
The opening of the compass is the radius. Find the radius of a circle whose diameter is 12 centimetres.
Example: For a circle of diameter 20 centimetres, the compass is opened to the radius, 20 divided by 2 equals 10 centimetres.
steps: The needle is at the centre and the pencil is on the circle, so the opening of the compass is the radius.
The radius is half the diameter. 12 divided by 2 equals 6.
The needle point and pencil tip should be 6 centimetres apart.

G4A_CIRCLE_003.q: A circle has a radius of 8 centimetres. How long is the longest chord that can be drawn in this circle?
hints: A chord joins two points on a circle. Think about which chord is the longest of all.
The longest chord passes through the centre, so it is the diameter. Find the diameter when the radius is 8 centimetres.
Example: In a circle of radius 5 centimetres, the longest chord is the diameter, 2 times 5 equals 10 centimetres.
steps: The longest chord of a circle is the one through the centre, which is the diameter.
The diameter is twice the radius. 2 times 8 equals 16.
The longest chord is 16 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_004.q: A circle has a radius of 6 centimetres. Point P is 4 centimetres away from the centre of the circle. Where is point P?
options: At the centre of the circle
hints: Every point on a circle is exactly one radius away from the centre. Compare the point's distance with the radius.
Is 4 centimetres less than, equal to, or more than the radius of 6 centimetres?
Example: A circle has radius 5 centimetres and a point is 9 centimetres from the centre. Since 9 is more than 5, that point is outside the circle.
steps: Points on the circle are exactly 6 centimetres from the centre.
Point P is 4 centimetres from the centre, and 4 is less than 6.
A point closer to the centre than the radius lies inside the circle, so P is inside the circle.

G4A_CIRCLE_005.q: O is the centre of a circle. A and B are two different points on the circle. If O A equals 7 centimetres, how long is O B?
hints: Think about what kind of line joins the centre of a circle to a point on the circle.
O A and O B both go from the centre to the circle, so both are radii. What do you know about all the radii of one circle?
Example: In a circle with centre C, if C P equals 4 centimetres and Q is also on the circle, then C Q is also a radius, so C Q equals 4 centimetres.
steps: O A joins the centre to a point on the circle, so O A is a radius.
O B also joins the centre to a point on the circle, so O B is a radius too.
All radii of a circle are equal, so O B equals 7 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_006.q: Four equal circles, each of radius 3 centimetres, are drawn in a straight row so that each circle touches the next one. What is the distance from the centre of the first circle to the centre of the last circle?
hints: When two equal circles touch, think about how far apart their centres are.
The centres of two touching circles are one radius plus one radius apart. Find that distance for radius 3 centimetres.

Example: Three circles of radius 2 centimetres touch in a row. Neighbouring centres are 4 centimetres apart, and there are 2 gaps from first to last, so the distance is 2 times 4, which is 8 centimetres.
steps: Centres of neighbouring circles are two radii apart. 3 plus 3 equals 6.
From the first centre to the fourth centre there are 3 gaps.
Multiply. 3 times 6 equals 18.
The distance between the first and last centres is 18 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_007.q: Six round bangles, each of radius 4 centimetres, are placed in a straight row on a table so that each bangle touches the next. How long is the row from end to end?
hints: Each bangle takes up its full width in the row. Think about which length of a circle is its width.
The width of one bangle is its diameter. Find the diameter when the radius is 4 centimetres.
Example: Five coins of radius 1 centimetre in a row. Each coin is 2 centimetres wide, so the row is 5 times 2, which is 10 centimetres long.
steps: Each bangle is one diameter wide. 2 times 4 equals 8.
There are 6 bangles in the row. 6 times 8 equals 48.
The row is 48 centimetres long.

G4A_CIRCLE_008.q: A circle is drawn inside a square of side 10 centimetres so that it just touches all four sides of the square. What is the radius of the circle?
hints: Picture the circle fitting snugly in the square. Think about which length of the circle stretches from one side of the square to the opposite side.
The circle reaches from one side to the opposite side, so its diameter equals the side of the square, 10 centimetres.
Example: A circle just fits in a square of side 8 centimetres. Its diameter is 8 centimetres, so its radius is 4 centimetres.
steps: The circle touches opposite sides of the square, so its diameter equals the side of the square.
The diameter is 10 centimetres.
The radius is half the diameter. 10 divided by 2 equals 5.
The radius of the circle is 5 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_009.q: A circle of radius 6 centimetres fits exactly inside a square, touching all four sides. What is the perimeter of the square?
hints: First find the side of the square from the circle, then find the distance around the square.
The side of the square equals the diameter of the circle. Find the diameter when the radius is 6 centimetres.
Example: A circle of radius 2 centimetres fits exactly in a square. The side is 4 centimetres, so the perimeter is 4 times 4, which is 16 centimetres.
steps: The side of the square equals the diameter. 2 times 6 equals 12.
A square has 4 equal sides. 4 times 12 equals 48.
The perimeter of the square is 48 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_010.q: Two coins lie flat on a table and touch each other. The radius of one coin is 5 centimetres and the radius of the other is 3 centimetres. How far apart are their centres?
hints: Imagine a straight line from one centre to the other. It passes through the point where the coins touch.
The line goes from the first centre to the touching point, one radius, then on to the second centre, the other radius.
Example: Circles of radius 4 centimetres and 2 centimetres touch side by side. Their centres are 4 plus 2, which is 6 centimetres apart.
steps: The line joining the centres passes through the point where the coins touch.
It is made of the radius of one coin and the radius of the other.
Add the two radii. 5 plus 3 equals 8.
The centres are 8 centimetres apart.

G4A_CIRCLE_011.q: Two circles are drawn with the same centre. The radius of the big circle is 9 centimetres and the radius of the small circle is 5 centimetres. How wide is the ring between the two circles?
hints: Walk in a straight line from the centre outwards. You cross the small circle first and then the big circle.
The width of the ring is how much farther the big circle is from the centre than the small circle.
Example: Circles with the same centre have radii 10 centimetres and 7 centimetres. The ring between them is 10 minus 7, which is 3 centimetres wide.
steps: Going out from the centre, the small circle is 5 centimetres away and the big circle is 9 centimetres away.
The ring is the gap between them. 9 minus 5 equals 4.
The ring is 4 centimetres wide.

G4A_CIRCLE_012.q: The diameter of a circle is 12 centimetres longer than its radius. What is the radius of the circle?
hints: A diameter is made of two radii. Think about what is left when you take one radius away from the diameter.
Diameter equals radius plus radius. If the diameter is also radius plus 12 centimetres, what must the second radius be?
Example: A diameter is 5 centimetres longer than its radius. Since the diameter is radius plus radius, the extra part is one radius, so the radius is 5 centimetres.
steps: The diameter is two radii: radius plus radius.
We are told the diameter is radius plus 12 centimetres.
Comparing the two, the second radius must be the extra 12 centimetres.
Check: the diameter is 24 centimetres, and it is 12 centimetres longer than the radius. 24 minus 12 equals 12.
The radius is 12 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_013.q: A circle has a radius of 6 centimetres. Which of these lengths can not be the length of a chord of this circle?
hints: A chord joins two points on the circle. Think about how long the longest possible chord is.
The longest chord is the diameter. Find the diameter when the radius is 6 centimetres.
Example: In a circle of radius 5 centimetres the longest chord is 10 centimetres, so a chord of 11 centimetres is not possible, but chords of 3 centimetres or 10 centimetres are.
steps: The longest chord is the diameter. 2 times 6 equals 12.
So a chord can be any length up to 12 centimetres, but never longer.
4 centimetres, 9 centimetres and 12 centimetres are all possible. The length that cannot be a chord is 13 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_014.q: A rectangular tray is 20 centimetres long and 8 centimetres wide. Round biscuits of radius 2 centimetres are laid flat on it in straight rows, touching each other but not overlapping. What is the greatest number of biscuits that fit on the tray?
hints: Each round biscuit needs a square space as wide as the biscuit. Find how many fit along the length and along the width.
The width of one biscuit is its diameter. Find the diameter when the radius is 2 centimetres.
Example: A tray 12 centimetres by 6 centimetres holds circles of radius 3 centimetres. Each is 6 centimetres wide, so 2 fit along the length and 1 along the width: 2 times 1 equals 2 circles.
steps: Each biscuit is one diameter wide. 2 times 2 equals 4.
Biscuits along the length. 20 divided by 4 equals 5.
Rows along the width. 8 divided by 4 equals 2.
Multiply. 5 times 2 equals 10.
The tray holds 10 biscuits.

G4A_CIRCLE_015.q: A piece of wire is bent to make a circle of radius 7 centimetres. The same wire is straightened and bent again to make a square. What is the side of the square? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: The length of the wire does not change. It is the distance around the circle, and then the distance around the square.
Find the circumference of the circle: 2 times 22 over 7 times 7.
Example: A wire makes a circle of radius 14 centimetres. Its length is 2 times 22 over 7 times 14, which is 88 centimetres. Bent into a square, each side is 88 divided by 4, which is 22 centimetres.
steps: The length of the wire is the circumference of the circle. 2 times 22 over 7 times 7 equals 44.
The same 44 centimetres of wire goes around the square.
A square has 4 equal sides. 44 divided by 4 equals 11.
The side of the square is 11 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_016.q: The radius of a big circle is equal to the diameter of a small circle. The radius of the small circle is 3 centimetres. What is the diameter of the big circle?
hints: Go one step at a time: small radius, small diameter, big radius, big diameter.
Find the diameter of the small circle first: twice 3 centimetres.
Example: A small circle has radius 2 centimetres, so its diameter is 4 centimetres. A big circle with radius 4 centimetres has diameter 8 centimetres.
steps: Diameter of the small circle. 2 times 3 equals 6.
This is the radius of the big circle, so the big radius is 6 centimetres.
Diameter of the big circle. 2 times 6 equals 12.
The diameter of the big circle is 12 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_017.q: Three equal circles with centres A, B and C each have a radius of 4 centimetres. Each circle touches the other two. What is the perimeter of triangle A B C?
hints: Each side of the triangle joins the centres of two touching circles. Find the length of one side first.
When two circles touch, the distance between their centres is one radius plus the other radius: 4 plus 4.
Example: Three circles of radius 5 centimetres touch each other. Each side of the triangle of centres is 10 centimetres, so its perimeter is 3 times 10, which is 30 centimetres.
steps: Each side joins two centres of touching circles. 4 plus 4 equals 8.
The triangle has 3 such sides. 3 times 8 equals 24.
The perimeter of triangle A B C is 24 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_018.q: Ten equal circles are drawn inside a rectangle in 2 rows of 5. Each circle touches the circles next to it, and the outer circles touch the sides of the rectangle. The perimeter of the rectangle is 84 centimetres. What is the radius of each circle?
hints: Write the length and the width of the rectangle as a number of diameters, then use the perimeter.
The length is 5 diameters and the width is 2 diameters. How many diameters make up half of the perimeter?

Example: Six circles in 2 rows of 3 fill a rectangle of perimeter 40 centimetres. Length plus width equals 3 plus 2, which is 5 diameters, or 20 centimetres, so a diameter is 4 centimetres and the radius is 2 centimetres.
steps: The length is 5 diameters and the width is 2 diameters.
Length plus width is half the perimeter. 84 divided by 2 equals 42.
Length plus width is 7 diameters. 42 divided by 7 equals 6.
The radius is half the diameter. 6 divided by 2 equals 3.
The radius of each circle is 3 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_019.q: A small circle of radius 3 centimetres lies inside a big circle of radius 10 centimetres and touches it at exactly one point. How far apart are the centres of the two circles?
hints: Draw a line from the big centre to the touching point. The small circle's centre lies on this line.
From the big centre to the touching point is 10 centimetres. From the small centre to the same point is 3 centimetres.
Example: A circle of radius 2 centimetres touches a circle of radius 8 centimetres from inside. The centres are 8 minus 2, which is 6 centimetres apart.
steps: The big centre, the small centre and the touching point lie on one straight line.
The big centre is 10 centimetres from the touching point, and the small centre is 3 centimetres from it.
The distance between the centres is the difference. 10 minus 3 equals 7.
The centres are 7 centimetres apart.

G4A_CIRCLE_020.q: Three circles of radii 2 centimetres, 3 centimetres and 4 centimetres are drawn in a row with their centres on one straight line. The middle circle, of radius 3 centimetres, touches the other two. What is the distance from the centre of the first circle to the centre of the last circle?
hints: Travel along the line from the first centre to the last centre and note which parts of each circle you cross.
You cross one radius of the first circle, then the whole middle circle, then one radius of the last circle.
Example: Circles of radii 1 centimetre, 2 centimetres and 5 centimetres in a row. From first centre to last centre: 1 plus, 2 plus 2, plus 5 equals 10 centimetres.
steps: From the first centre to its edge is one radius, 2 centimetres.
Crossing the whole middle circle is its diameter. 2 times 3 equals 6.
From the edge of the last circle to its centre is one radius, 4 centimetres.
Add the three parts. 2 plus 6 plus 4 equals 12.
The distance between the first and last centres is 12 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_021.q: The circumference of a circle is 88 centimetres. The circle fits exactly inside a square, touching all four sides. What is the side of the square? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: Work backwards from the circumference to the radius, then think about how the circle sits in the square.
Circumference equals 2 times 22 over 7 times radius. So 44 over 7 times the radius is 88.
Example: A circle has circumference 44 centimetres. Then 44 over 7 times the radius is 44, so the radius is 7 centimetres. The square around it has side equal to the diameter, 14 centimetres.
steps: The circumference is 2 times 22 over 7 times the radius. 44 over 7 times 14 equals 88.
So the radius is 14 centimetres.
The side of the square equals the diameter. 2 times 14 equals 28.
The side of the square is 28 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_022.q: A circle of radius 7 centimetres is cut out of a square sheet of paper of side 14 centimetres. What is the area of the paper that is left? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: The paper left is the square with the circle taken away. Find two areas.
Find the area of the square first: 14 times 14.
Example: A circle of area 154 square centimetres is cut from a square sheet of side 20 centimetres. The square is 400 square centimetres, so 400 minus 154 equals 246 square centimetres is left.
steps: Area of the square. 14 times 14 equals 196.
Area of the circle. 22 over 7 times 7 times 7 equals 154.
Take the circle away from the square. 196 minus 154 equals 42.
The area of paper left is 42 square centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_023.q: Five points are marked on a circle. Every pair of points is joined by a straight line. How many chords are drawn?
hints: Each chord joins two of the points. Count the pairs in an orderly way so that none is counted twice.
Call the points P, Q, R, S, T. Start by counting the chords from P to each of the other four points.
Example: With 4 points on a circle, the first point joins 3 others, the next joins 2 new ones, and the next joins 1 new one: 3 plus 2 plus 1 equals 6 chords.
steps: From the first point, 4 chords go to the other points.
From the second point, 3 new chords can be drawn, then 2 from the third and 1 from the fourth.
Add them. 4 plus 3 plus 2 plus 1 equals 10.
10 chords are drawn.

G4A_CIRCLE_024.q: Two square trays each have a side of 24 centimetres. The first tray is exactly filled by 9 equal round plates in 3 rows of 3. The second tray is exactly filled by 16 equal round plates in 4 rows of 4. In each tray the plates touch each other and the sides. How much longer is the radius of a plate in the first tray than in the second tray?
hints: In each tray, the plates in one row share the 24 centimetre side equally. Find each plate's diameter, then its radius.
In the first tray, 3 plates fit across 24 centimetres. Find the diameter of one plate: 24 divided by 3.

Example: A 20 centimetre square tray holds 2 plates across, so each is 10 centimetres wide with radius 5 centimetres. If it holds 5 plates across, each is 4 centimetres wide with radius 2 centimetres. The radii differ by 5 minus 2, which is 3 centimetres.
steps: First tray: 3 plates across. 24 divided by 3 equals 8.
So the radius of a plate in the first tray is 4 centimetres.
Second tray: 4 plates across. 24 divided by 4 equals 6.
So the radius of a plate in the second tray is 3 centimetres.
Compare the radii. 4 minus 3 equals 1.
The radius in the first tray is longer by 1 centimetre.

G4A_CIRCLE_025.q: A wire 132 centimetres long is cut into 3 equal pieces. Each piece is bent to make a circle. What is the radius of each circle? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: Each piece of wire becomes the distance around one circle. Find the length of one piece first.
Divide 132 centimetres by 3 to find the length of one piece.
Example: A wire 176 centimetres long is cut into 2 equal pieces of 88 centimetres. For a circle, 44 over 7 times the radius is 88, so the radius is 14 centimetres.
steps: Length of one piece. 132 divided by 3 equals 44.
This is the circumference of one circle: 2 times 22 over 7 times the radius is 44.
A radius of 7 centimetres fits. 2 times 22 over 7 times 7 equals 44.
The radius of each circle is 7 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_026.q: Twelve equal circles are drawn inside a rectangle in 3 rows of 4. Each circle touches the circles next to it, and the circles on the outside touch the sides of the rectangle. The area of the rectangle is 432 square centimetres. What is the radius of each circle?
hints: Each circle sits snugly inside its own little square, and the twelve little squares fill the rectangle exactly. Work backwards from the area.
Share the area of the rectangle equally among the 12 little squares. Then find the side of one little square, and think about how that side is related to the circle inside it.

Similar problem: 6 equal circles in 2 rows of 3 fill a rectangle of area 96 square centimetres. Each little square has area 96 divided by 6, which is 16 square centimetres, so its side is 4 centimetres. That side is the diameter of a circle, so the radius is 2 centimetres.
steps: The rectangle is made of 12 equal little squares, one around each circle. 432 divided by 12 equals 36.
A square of area 36 square centimetres has a side of 6 centimetres. 6 times 6 equals 36.
The side of the little square is the diameter of the circle inside it.
The radius is half the diameter. 6 divided by 2 equals 3.
So the radius of each circle is 3 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_027.q: A round pond has a radius of 7 metres. A path 7 metres wide runs all the way around the pond. What is the area of the path? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: The path is a ring. A ring is what is left when a small circle is taken out of a bigger circle with the same centre.
Find the radius of the big circle made by the pond and the path together. It reaches from the centre of the pond to the outer edge of the path.

Similar problem: a pond of radius 14 metres with a path 7 metres wide. The big circle has radius 21 metres and area 22 over 7 times 21 times 21, which is 1386 square metres. The pond has area 22 over 7 times 14 times 14, which is 616 square metres. The path is 1386 minus 616, which is 770 square metres.
steps: The pond and path together make a big circle. Find its radius. 7 plus 7 equals 14.
Find the area of the big circle. 22 over 7 times 14 times 14 equals 616.
Find the area of the pond. 22 over 7 times 7 times 7 equals 154.
Take the pond out of the big circle. 616 minus 154 equals 462.
So the area of the path is 462 square metres.

G4A_CIRCLE_028.q: When the radius of a circle is made twice as long, its circumference becomes 88 centimetres longer than before. What was the radius of the circle at the start? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: Think about what happens to the circumference when the radius is doubled. You can also test each choice: find the circumference before and after, and see how much it grows.
Try a radius of 7 centimetres. The circumference is 44 centimetres. With a radius of 14 centimetres it is 88 centimetres. Find how much it has grown, and compare with what the question says.

Similar problem: doubling the radius makes the circumference 132 centimetres longer. Doubling the radius doubles the circumference, so the extra part equals the old circumference, 132 centimetres. Since 2 times 22 over 7 times 21 equals 132, the radius at the start was 21 centimetres.
steps: When the radius is doubled, the circumference is doubled too.
So the extra length is exactly as long as the old circumference: the old circumference is 88 centimetres.
Find the radius of a circle with circumference 88 centimetres. 2 times 22 over 7 times 14 equals 88.
Check: the new radius is 28 centimetres, and the circumference has grown by 88 centimetres. 2 times 22 over 7 times 28 equals 176 and 176 minus 88 equals 88.
So the radius at the start was 14 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_029.q: Seven points are marked on a circle. Each point is joined by a straight chord to every other point, except the two points right next to it. How many chords are drawn?
hints: Work out how many chords leave one point. Then think carefully before you multiply: every chord has two ends.
From one point there are 6 other points. Two of them are its neighbours, so find how many chords start at this point.

Similar problem: five points on a circle, each joined to every point except its two neighbours. Each point sends out 2 chords, and 5 times 2 equals 10. But every chord has been counted from both of its ends, so there are 10 divided by 2, which is 5 chords.
steps: From each point, take away the point itself and its two neighbours. 7 minus 3 equals 4.
Seven points each send out 4 chords. 7 times 4 equals 28.
Each chord joins two points, so it has been counted twice.
Halve the total. 28 divided by 2 equals 14.
So 14 chords are drawn.

G4A_CIRCLE_030.q: Eight points are marked on a circle, equally spaced all the way round. Every pair of points is joined by a chord. How many of these chords are not diameters of the circle?
hints: Count all the chords first, in an orderly way. Then decide which chords pass through the centre, and be careful not to count any of those twice.
The first point is joined to 7 others, the second to 6 new ones, and so on. A chord is a diameter only when it joins a point to the point exactly opposite.

Similar problem: six equally spaced points. The chords number 5 plus 4 plus 3 plus 2 plus 1, which is 15. The six points make 3 opposite pairs, so 3 chords are diameters. That leaves 15 minus 3, which is 12 chords that are not diameters.
steps: Count all the chords. 7 plus 6 plus 5 plus 4 plus 3 plus 2 plus 1 equals 28.
A chord is a diameter when it joins two opposite points.
Eight points make 4 opposite pairs, so there are 4 diameters. 8 divided by 2 equals 4.
Take the diameters away from all the chords. 28 minus 4 equals 24.
So 24 of the chords are not diameters.

G4A_CIRCLE_031.q: A small circle is drawn inside a big circle. The small circle touches the big circle at exactly one point, and it also passes through the centre of the big circle. The diameter of the big circle is 24 centimetres. How far apart are the centres of the two circles?
hints: Imagine a straight line from the point where the circles touch to the centre of the big circle. Think about what this line is for each of the two circles.
That line is a radius of the big circle. It also goes right across the small circle, from one side to the other through its centre.

Similar problem: the big circle has diameter 40 centimetres. Its radius is 20 centimetres, and this is the diameter of the small circle. The small circle's centre is halfway along, 10 centimetres from the big centre. So the centres are 10 centimetres apart.
steps: Find the radius of the big circle. 24 divided by 2 equals 12.
The line from the touching point to the big centre is 12 centimetres long, and it is a diameter of the small circle.
The centre of the small circle is halfway along this line. 12 divided by 2 equals 6.
So the small centre is 6 centimetres from the big centre.
So the centres of the two circles are 6 centimetres apart.

G4A_CIRCLE_032.q: Three coins of different sizes lie flat on a table, and each coin touches the other two. The distances between their centres are 7 centimetres, 8 centimetres and 9 centimetres. What is the radius of the largest coin?
hints: When two coins touch, the distance between their centres is one radius plus the other radius. Think about what you get if you add all three distances.
Add 7, 8 and 9. In that total every radius has been counted twice. Halve it to find the three radii added together.

Similar problem: the distances are 5 centimetres, 6 centimetres and 7 centimetres. They add up to 18 centimetres, so the three radii add up to 9 centimetres. The two smaller coins are 5 centimetres apart, so the largest coin has radius 9 minus 5, which is 4 centimetres.
steps: Add the three distances. Each radius is counted twice. 7 plus 8 plus 9 equals 24.
Halve to get the three radii added together. 24 divided by 2 equals 12.
The two smaller coins have the closest centres, 7 centimetres apart. Take their radii away. 12 minus 7 equals 5.
Check: the radii are 3 centimetres, 4 centimetres and 5 centimetres. 3 plus 4 equals 7 and 3 plus 5 equals 8 and 4 plus 5 equals 9.
So the radius of the largest coin is 5 centimetres.

G4A_CIRCLE_033.q: Two round tins, each of radius 7 centimetres, stand on a table touching each other. A ribbon is pulled tight around the two tins together. It goes straight across from one tin to the other on both sides, and it curves around the outer half of each tin. How long is the ribbon? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: Break the ribbon into its parts: the straight parts and the curved parts. Find each part and add them up.
Each straight part runs from the widest point of one tin to the widest point of the other, so it is as long as the distance between the two centres. The two curved parts are half circles.

Similar problem: two tins of radius 14 centimetres. The centres are 28 centimetres apart, so the two straight parts are 28 centimetres each. The two half circles make one whole circle of 2 times 22 over 7 times 14, which is 88 centimetres. The ribbon is 28 plus 28 plus 88, which is 144 centimetres long.
steps: The tins touch, so their centres are two radii apart. Each straight part is this long. 7 plus 7 equals 14.
There are two straight parts. 2 times 14 equals 28.
The two curved parts are half circles, which together make one whole circle. 2 times 22 over 7 times 7 equals 44.
Add the straight parts and the curved parts. 28 plus 44 equals 72.
So the ribbon is 72 centimetres long.

G4A_CIRCLE_034.q: The hour hand of a wall clock is 7 centimetres long. How far does the tip of the hour hand travel in one full day of 24 hours? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: The tip of the hand moves along a circle. Before you calculate, think about how many times the hour hand goes all the way round in a whole day.
The hour hand takes 12 hours to go once round the clock face. Work out how many times it goes round in 24 hours.

Similar problem: a minute hand 21 centimetres long, over 2 hours. The minute hand goes round once every hour, so twice in 2 hours. One round is 2 times 22 over 7 times 21, which is 132 centimetres, so the tip travels 2 times 132, which is 264 centimetres.
steps: The tip moves on a circle of radius 7 centimetres. Find the distance once round. 2 times 22 over 7 times 7 equals 44.
The hour hand goes once round in 12 hours. Find how many times it goes round in a day. 24 divided by 12 equals 2.
Multiply the distance once round by the number of rounds. 2 times 44 equals 88.
So the tip of the hour hand travels 88 centimetres.

PYQ_2019_Q15.q: Eight circles of equal diameters are drawn in a rectangle in 2 rows of 4. Each circle touches the circles next to it and the nearest sides of the rectangle at one point only. The radius of each circle is 6 centimetres. Find the perimeter of the rectangle.
hints: The circles fill the rectangle exactly, so its length and breadth can be counted in circle widths. Then go all the way round the rectangle.
Find the diameter of one circle: it is twice the radius of 6 centimetres. The length of the rectangle is 4 diameters and the breadth is 2 diameters.

Similar example: 6 equal circles of radius 5 centimetres sit in a rectangle in 2 rows of 3. The diameter is 10 centimetres, so the length is 30 centimetres and the breadth is 20 centimetres. The perimeter is 2 times, 30 plus 20, which is 100 centimetres.
steps: The diameter of each circle is twice the radius. 2 times 6 equals 12.
The length holds 4 circles and the breadth holds 2 circles. 4 times 12 equals 48. 2 times 12 equals 24.
Add the length and the breadth, then double it to go round all four sides. 2 times, 48 plus 24, equals 144.
The perimeter of the rectangle is 144 centimetres.

Q_CH20_011_V04.q: A circle has a radius of 21 centimetres. What is its area? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: This asks for the area of a circle, the space inside it. The rule uses pi and the radius.
Area equals pi times radius times radius. Put 21 in for the radius and 22 over 7 for pi. Try dividing 21 by 7 first.
A similar example: a circle with radius 7 centimetres. Area equals 22 over 7 times 7 times 7. First 7 divided by 7 equals 1. Then 22 times 1 times 7 equals 154. The area is 154 square centimetres.
steps: The area of a circle is pi times radius times radius. The radius is 21 centimetres.
Divide 21 by 7 first to make the sum easy. 21 divided by 7 equals 3.
Now multiply 22 by 3, then by 21. 22 times 3 times 21 equals 1386.
The area is 1386 square centimetres. 22 over 7 times 21 times 21 equals 1386.

Q_CH20_011_V05.q: A circle has a radius of 35 centimetres. What is its circumference? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: This asks for the circumference, the distance all the way around the circle. The rule uses pi and the radius.
Circumference equals 2 times pi times radius. Put 35 in for the radius and 22 over 7 for pi. Try dividing 35 by 7 first.

A similar example: a circle with radius 21 centimetres. Circumference equals 2 times 22 over 7 times 21. First 21 divided by 7 equals 3. Then 2 times 22 times 3 equals 132. The circumference is 132 centimetres.
steps: The circumference of a circle is 2 times pi times radius. The radius is 35 centimetres.
Divide 35 by 7 first to make the sum easy. 35 divided by 7 equals 5.
Now multiply 2 by 22, then by 5. 2 times 22 times 5 equals 220.
The circumference is 220 centimetres. 2 times 22 over 7 times 35 equals 220.

Q_CH21_001.q: A circle is a set of all points that are equidistant from a fixed point called the:
hints: All points on a circle are the same distance from one special point.
This fixed point in the middle is called the centre.
The centre is not on the circle, it's inside it!
steps: A circle is defined by its centre and radius.
The fixed point is the centre.

Q_CH21_003.q: If the radius of a circle is 9.5 centimetres, what is its diameter?
hints: The diameter is always twice the radius.
D equals 2 times r, which is 2 times 9.5
That equals 19 centimetres
steps: D equals 2 r. D equals 2 times 9.5.
D equals 19 centimetres

Q_CH21_004.q: The longest chord of a circle is called the:
hints: A chord is a line segment with both endpoints on the circle.
The longest possible chord passes through the centre.
A chord through the centre is a diameter. It's the longest chord.
steps: A chord through the centre is the longest chord possible.
Answer: diameter

Q_CH21_005.q: How many axes of symmetry does a circle have?
hints: Every diameter divides the circle into two equal halves.
How many diameters can you draw? You can draw one in any direction!
Infinite diameters means infinite axes of symmetry.
steps: Every diameter is an axis of symmetry.
Infinite diameters, so infinite axes.

Q_CH21_006.q: Find the circumference of a circle with radius 21 centimetres. Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: Circumference equals 2 times pi times r, which is 2 times 22 over 7 times 21.
Simplify: 21 divided by 7 equals 3. So C equals 2 times 22 times 3.
That equals 132 centimetres.
steps: C equals 2 pi r, which is 2 times 22 over 7 times 21
21 divided by 7 equals 3. So C equals 2 times 22 times 3, which is 132
Circumference equals 132 centimetres

Q_CH21_006_V01.q: A circle has a radius of 28 centimetres. What is its area? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: This asks for the area of a circle, the space inside it. The rule uses pi and the radius.
Area equals pi times radius times radius. Put 28 in for the radius and 22 over 7 for pi. Try dividing 28 by 7 first.

A similar example: a circle with radius 21 centimetres. Area equals 22 over 7 times 21 times 21. First 21 divided by 7 equals 3. Then 22 times 3 times 21 equals 1386. The area is 1386 square centimetres.
steps: The area of a circle is pi times radius times radius. The radius is 28 centimetres.
Divide 28 by 7 first to make the sum easy. 28 divided by 7 equals 4.
Now multiply 22 by 4, then by 28. 22 times 4 times 28 equals 2464.
The area is 2464 square centimetres. 22 over 7 times 28 times 28 equals 2464.

Q_CH21_006_V05.q: A circle has a radius of 14 centimetres. What is its circumference? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: This asks for the circumference, the distance all the way around the circle. The rule uses pi and the radius.
Circumference equals 2 times pi times radius. Put 14 in for the radius and 22 over 7 for pi. Try dividing 14 by 7 first.

A similar example: a circle with radius 21 centimetres. Circumference equals 2 times 22 over 7 times 21. First 21 divided by 7 equals 3. Then 2 times 22 times 3 equals 132. The circumference is 132 centimetres.
steps: The circumference of a circle is 2 times pi times radius. The radius is 14 centimetres.
Divide 14 by 7 first to make the sum easy. 14 divided by 7 equals 2.
Now multiply 2 by 22, then by 2. 2 times 22 times 2 equals 88.
The circumference is 88 centimetres. 2 times 22 over 7 times 14 equals 88.

Q_CH21_006_V07.q: A circle has a radius of 28 centimetres. What is its circumference? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: This asks for the circumference, the distance all the way around the circle. The rule uses pi and the radius.
Circumference equals 2 times pi times radius. Put 28 in for the radius and 22 over 7 for pi. Try dividing 28 by 7 first.

A similar example: a circle with radius 21 centimetres. Circumference equals 2 times 22 over 7 times 21. First 21 divided by 7 equals 3. Then 2 times 22 times 3 equals 132. The circumference is 132 centimetres.
steps: The circumference of a circle is 2 times pi times radius. The radius is 28 centimetres.
Divide 28 by 7 first to make the sum easy. 28 divided by 7 equals 4.
Now multiply 2 by 22, then by 4. 2 times 22 times 4 equals 176.
The circumference is 176 centimetres. 2 times 22 over 7 times 28 equals 176.

Q_CH21_006_V09.q: A circle has a radius of 7 centimetres. What is its circumference? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: This asks for the circumference, the distance all the way around the circle. The rule uses pi and the radius.
Circumference equals 2 times pi times radius. Put 7 in for the radius and 22 over 7 for pi. Try dividing 7 by 7 first.

A similar example: a circle with radius 21 centimetres. Circumference equals 2 times 22 over 7 times 21. First 21 divided by 7 equals 3. Then 2 times 22 times 3 equals 132. The circumference is 132 centimetres.
steps: The circumference of a circle is 2 times pi times radius. The radius is 7 centimetres.
Divide 7 by 7 first to make the sum easy. 7 divided by 7 equals 1.
Now multiply 2 by 22, then by 1. 2 times 22 times 1 equals 44.
The circumference is 44 centimetres. 2 times 22 over 7 times 7 equals 44.

Q_CH21_007.q: Find the circumference of a circle with diameter 14 centimetres. Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: Circumference equals pi times d, which is 22 over 7 times 14.
14 divided by 7 equals 2. So C equals 22 times 2, which is 44.
Circumference equals 44 centimetres.
steps: C equals pi d, which is 22 over 7 times 14
14 divided by 7 equals 2. C equals 22 times 2, which is 44
Circumference equals 44 centimetres

Q_CH21_007_V01.q: A circle has a radius of 35 centimetres. What is its area? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: This asks for the area of a circle, the space inside it. The rule uses pi and the radius.
Area equals pi times radius times radius. Put 35 in for the radius and 22 over 7 for pi. Try dividing 35 by 7 first.

A similar example: a circle with radius 21 centimetres. Area equals 22 over 7 times 21 times 21. First 21 divided by 7 equals 3. Then 22 times 3 times 21 equals 1386. The area is 1386 square centimetres.
steps: The area of a circle is pi times radius times radius. The radius is 35 centimetres.
Divide 35 by 7 first to make the sum easy. 35 divided by 7 equals 5.
Now multiply 22 by 5, then by 35. 22 times 5 times 35 equals 3850.
The area is 3850 square centimetres. 22 over 7 times 35 times 35 equals 3850.

Q_CH21_007_V05.q: A circle has a radius of 14 centimetres. What is its area? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: This asks for the area of a circle, the space inside it. The rule uses pi and the radius.
Area equals pi times radius times radius. Put 14 in for the radius and 22 over 7 for pi. Try dividing 14 by 7 first.

A similar example: a circle with radius 21 centimetres. Area equals 22 over 7 times 21 times 21. First 21 divided by 7 equals 3. Then 22 times 3 times 21 equals 1386. The area is 1386 square centimetres.
steps: The area of a circle is pi times radius times radius. The radius is 14 centimetres.
Divide 14 by 7 first to make the sum easy. 14 divided by 7 equals 2.
Now multiply 22 by 2, then by 14. 22 times 2 times 14 equals 616.
The area is 616 square centimetres. 22 over 7 times 14 times 14 equals 616.

Q_CH21_008.q: The circumference of a circle is 440 metres. Find its radius. Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: C equals 2 pi r. So r equals C divided by 2 pi, which is 440, divided by 2 times 22 over 7.
2 times 22 over 7 equals 44 over 7. So r equals 440 divided by 44 over 7, which is 440 times 7 over 44.
440 divided by 44 equals 10. 10 times 7 equals 70 metres.
steps: C equals 2 pi r, so r equals C over 2 pi. So r equals 440, divided by 2 times 22 over 7.
That equals 440 times 7 over 44, which is 10 times 7, which is 70
Radius equals 70 metres

Q_CH21_009.q: The circumference of a circular park is 176 metres. Find its diameter. Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: C equals pi d. So d equals C divided by pi, which is 176 divided by 22 over 7.
176 divided by 22 over 7 equals 176 times 7 over 22.
176 divided by 22 equals 8. 8 times 7 equals 56 metres.
steps: C equals pi d, so d equals C over pi. So d equals 176 divided by 22 over 7, which is 176 times 7 over 22.
176 divided by 22 equals 8. Then 8 times 7 equals 56.
Diameter equals 56 metres

Q_CH21_010.q: Find the area of a circle with radius 7 centimetres. Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: Area equals pi times r squared, which is 22 over 7 times 7 times 7.
One 7 cancels: 22 over 7 times 7 equals 22. Then 22 times 7 equals 154.
Area equals 154 square centimetres.
steps: A equals pi r squared, which is 22 over 7 times 7 squared. 22 over 7 times 7 times 7.
That equals 22 times 7, which is 154
Area equals 154 square centimetres

Q_CH21_011.q: Find the area of a circle with diameter 14 centimetres. Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: First find radius: r equals d over 2, which is 14 over 2, which is 7 centimetres.
Area equals pi r squared, which is 22 over 7 times 7 times 7, which is 154 square centimetres.
Same as the previous problem! Diameter 14, so radius 7, so area 154.
steps: R equals d over 2, which is 14 over 2, which is 7 centimetres
A equals pi r squared, which is 22 over 7 times 49, which is 154 square centimetres
Area equals 154 square centimetres

Q_CH21_012.q: A circular track has radius 35 metres. How far does a runner go in 3 laps? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: 1 lap equals the circumference, which is 2 pi r. That is 2 times 22 over 7 times 35.
35 divided by 7 equals 5. So C equals 2 times 22 times 5, which is 220 metres. That's 1 lap.
3 laps equals 3 times 220, which is 660 metres.
steps: 1 lap equals C, which is 2 pi r. That is 2 times 22 over 7 times 35, which is 220 metres. 2 times 22 times 5 equals 220.
3 laps equals 3 times 220, which is 660 metres

Q_CH21_012_V02.q: A circle has a radius of 7 centimetres. What is its area? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: This asks for the area of a circle, the space inside it. The rule uses pi and the radius.
Area equals pi times radius times radius. Put 7 in for the radius and 22 over 7 for pi. Try dividing 7 by 7 first.

A similar example: a circle with radius 21 centimetres. Area equals 22 over 7 times 21 times 21. First 21 divided by 7 equals 3. Then 22 times 3 times 21 equals 1386. The area is 1386 square centimetres.
steps: The area of a circle is pi times radius times radius. The radius is 7 centimetres.
Divide 7 by 7 first to make the sum easy. 7 divided by 7 equals 1.
Now multiply 22 by 1, then by 7. 22 times 1 times 7 equals 154.
The area is 154 square centimetres. 22 over 7 times 7 times 7 equals 154.

Q_CH21_014.q: A diameter divides a circle into two equal parts. Each part is called a:
hints: Semi means half. So semicircle means half circle.
A diameter passes through the centre and divides the circle into exactly 2 equal halves.
Each half is a semicircle.
steps: Diameter splits circle into 2 equal halves.
Answer: semicircle

Q_CH21_015.q: A wheel has diameter 28 centimetres. How many complete rotations will it make to cover 440 centimetres? Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: 1 rotation equals 1 circumference, which is pi d, which is 22 over 7 times 28.
28 divided by 7 equals 4. C equals 22 times 4, which is 88 centimetres per rotation.
Rotations equals 440 divided by 88, which is 5.
steps: C equals pi d, which is 22 over 7 times 28, which is 88 centimetres
Rotations equals 440 divided by 88, which is 5
5 complete rotations

Q_CH21_016.q: Circles that have the same centre but different radii are called:
hints: Concentric means: with the same centre.
Like rings on a target board, same centre, different sizes.
These are concentric circles.
steps: Same centre, plus different radii, gives concentric circles.
Answer: concentric circles

Q_CH21_017.q: The area of a circle is 616 square centimetres. Find its radius. Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: A equals pi r squared. So r squared equals A over pi, which is 616 divided by 22 over 7, which is 616 times 7 over 22.
616 divided by 22 equals 28. Then 28 times 7 equals 196. So r squared equals 196.
R equals the square root of 196, which is 14 centimetres.
steps: R squared equals A over pi, which is 616 times 7 over 22. R squared equals 616 times 7 over 22, which is 196.
R equals the square root of 196, which is 14
Radius equals 14 centimetres

Q_CH21_018.q: For a circle with radius 7 centimetres, which is larger numerically: the circumference or the area?
hints: C equals 2 pi r, which is 2 times 22 over 7 times 7, which is 44. A equals pi r squared, which is 22 over 7 times 49, which is 154.
Numerically: 154 is greater than 44.
The area, 154, is larger than the circumference, 44. But note: they have different units!
steps: C equals 44 centimetres. A equals 154 square centimetres.
154 is greater than 44 numerically.

Q_CH21_019.q: How many radii and diameters can a circle have?
hints: A radius can go from the centre to any point on the circle. How many points are on a circle?
Infinite points, so infinite radii. And since every diameter passes through the centre in any direction.
Infinite diameters too! Both are infinite.
steps: Infinite points on circle, so infinite radii
Infinite directions through centre, so infinite diameters
Both are infinite.

Q_CH21_020.q: Find the perimeter of a semicircle with diameter 14 centimetres. Use pi as 22 over 7.
hints: Perimeter of a semicircle equals half the circumference plus the diameter, the straight edge.
Half the circumference equals pi d over 2. That is 22 over 7 times 14 over 2, which is 22 over 7 times 7, or 22 centimetres.
Perimeter equals 22 plus 14, which is 36 centimetres.
steps: Curved part equals pi d over 2, which is 22 over 7 times 14 divided by 2, which is 22 centimetres. Pi d over 2 equals 22 over 7 times 7, which is 22.
Straight part equals diameter, which is 14 centimetres
Perimeter equals 22 plus 14, which is 36 centimetres
